passage: A screening group in the Fitzgerald laboratory identified a compound that suppresses aldose reductase activity in cell lysates. To learn how it acts, the group measured initial velocities of the purified enzyme at several glucose concentrations, with and without 20 µM compound. Assays were buffered at pH 7.4 and kept at 30 °C, and the enzyme concentration was held constant. The compound has no structural resemblance to glucose, and a preliminary docking study placed it in a hydrophobic pocket far from the catalytic residues. The researchers recorded velocities as µmol of product per minute and fit each data set to the Michaelis–Menten equation. They then compared the fitted constants with and without compound, expecting the pattern to reveal whether the compound binds the free enzyme, the enzyme–substrate complex, or both with equal affinity. Enzyme purity exceeded 95% by SDS-PAGE, and solvent carrier alone had no effect on activity. All procedures followed the laboratory's standard operating protocols, and raw data were archived before analysis.

options.A: The inhibited velocity exceeds the control velocity at the lowest [S]
options.B: The ratio falls steadily as [S] increases
options.C: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity is about the same at every [S]
options.D: The ratio of inhibited to control velocity rises steadily as [S] increases

questions.explanation: At each [S], v(inhibited)/v(control) = 1/5, so the compound lowers velocity by a constant factor.
questions.trap: Expecting inhibition to be strongest at low [S] or to change with [S] (as in competitive inhibition), when the inhibited/control ratio stays constant at every [S].

questions.stem: Which experiment would best confirm that the compound does not compete with substrate for the active site?

options.A: Show that the compound's structure matches the substrate
options.B: Show that Km increases linearly with compound concentration
options.C: Show that the compound's potency decreases as [S] increases
options.D: Show that raising [S] to very high levels does not restore the control Vmax

questions.explanation: Failure of high [S] to overcome inhibition indicates the inhibitor does not simply compete for the substrate-binding site.
questions.trap: Choosing a signature of competitive inhibition (potency falling as [S] rises, Km rising with inhibitor) or substrate resemblance, which is the opposite of what is asked.

questions.stem: If the uninhibited Vmax is 200 µmol/min, what is the apparent Vmax with the compound?
questions.explanation: Vmax,app = Vmax/α = 200/5 = 40 µmol/min, as seen in the saturating-substrate rows.
questions.trap: Multiplying Vmax by 5 (1000) or subtracting a small amount (195) instead of dividing 200 by the factor of 5 seen in the table.

questions.stem: Which statement about pure noncompetitive inhibition is INCORRECT?

options.A: The apparent Km increases because the inhibitor competes with substrate
options.C: The inhibitor can bind both free enzyme and enzyme–substrate complex
options.D: Lineweaver–Burk lines intersect on the x-axis

questions.explanation: Pure noncompetitive inhibitors leave Km unchanged. Because binding occurs at a distinct site, the lines in a double-reciprocal plot share an x-intercept (−1/Km).
questions.topic: Enzyme inhibition: trap on Km vs Vmax
questions.trap: Assuming every inhibitor raises apparent Km, which is true only for competitive inhibition; pure noncompetitive inhibition leaves Km unchanged.

questions.stem: Which cellular regulatory phenomenon most closely resembles this inhibition pattern?

options.A: Allosteric inhibition at a site distinct from the active site
options.B: Substrate-level competition by a structural analog
options.C: Product activation of the same enzyme by direct covalent change
options.D: Irreversible inhibition by transition-state mimicry at the active site

questions.explanation: Binding at a distinct regulatory (allosteric) site that lowers catalytic capacity reproduces the noncompetitive pattern, as with feedback inhibition in metabolic pathways.
questions.trap: Choosing substrate competition by a structural analog, which would raise Km, although the compound lacks substrate resemblance and Km is unchanged.
